description: We are AgroZone from Ukraine, scaling our HydroBrain smart irrigation AI into a NASA-powered ag-tool. Core team: Mykhailo Ivantsov & Yaroslava Stetsenko (Bioinformaticians & Biotechnologists blending wet-lab, NGS, and Python) and Alina Shevchenko (Data Analytics). Using NASA data, we want to help farms adapt to climate shifts. Innovate with us!
summary:
AGROZONE: Climate-Resilient Crop Rotation Planner
AGROZONE is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers plan crop rotations under a changing climate. Developed for the 2026 NASA Space Apps Challenge for "Field Shift: Adapting Farms with NASA Data", it turns complex Earth-observation data into practical, field-level insights.
A farmer selects a field on the map or drops a pin, enters basic soil and slope information, and compares their current rotation with three alternatives. AGROZONE evaluates each option using more than 40 years of NASA POWER weather data, together with SRTM elevation, SMAP soil moisture, MODIS vegetation data, ECOSTRESS land-surface temperature, and SoilGrids soil information.
Users can adjust temperature and rainfall sliders to stress-test rotations under hotter, drier, or more unpredictable conditions. This information remains in the browser and can be uploaded in PDF format.
Instead of giving one generic recommendation, AGROZONE shows the trade-offs behind each rotation: expected income, water use, soil cover, nitrogen balance, drought and frost risk, and periods without plant cover. This helps farmers choose rotations that protect soil health, conserve water, and maintain stable yields over time.
details:
What does it do and how does it work? 

AGROZONE is a web-based decision-support tool that helps farmers plan crop rotations under a changing climate. You can explore it at https://agrozone-964318999047.europe-central2.run.app/ by following these steps:

1. Select your field. Click Start with your field, then place a pin on the map, draw your field boundary, or enter coordinates. Specify the area and choose whether you are working with a farm field or a garden plot. Use automatic soil and terrain settings, select them manually, or enter your own soil test data.
2. Enter your current crop rotation. Click Next and select a predefined rotation or build your own sequence of two to five crops. You can change each crop, add or remove years, and include cover crops between main crops. This rotation becomes the reference for comparison.
3. Choose your priorities. Select the outcome that matters most: balanced performance, higher margin, water efficiency, soil conservation, or a stable harvest. You can also set a minimum acceptable income, enable protection against greater crop-failure risk, and decide whether cover crops may be suggested.
4. Set your practical constraints. Specify whether your field is rainfed or irrigated, then select your tillage method, mulch, residue management, organic fertiliser, and available equipment. Exclude crops you cannot grow or do not want to consider. You can also adjust prices, costs, and yields.
5. Run the comparison. Click Compare rotations to evaluate your current rotation alongside proposed alternatives using historical weather and field conditions.
6. Explore the results. Compare estimated income, yield stability, water requirements, and soil impacts. Review the trade-offs to see which rotation best matches your priorities and practical limits. Return to the setup steps, change your choices, and run the comparison again to explore different scenarios.

The interface is available in English and Ukrainian, with Simple and Advanced modes.

What benefits does it have?

For the Farmer

  • Tailored to your exact field. The program uses 42 years of NASA POWER weather data for your specific coordinates, along with local soil type and slope, rather than broad regional averages.
  • Side-by-side comparisons, not a single answer. Your current crop rotation is placed right next to three alternatives so you can clearly see the trade-offs in water, income, yield, and soil health.
  • Stress-tested for bad years. Every option is modeled for both normal and unfavorable seasons. Interactive climate sliders (less rain, higher temperatures) show which rotation can handle extreme conditions.
  • Plain-language insights. Each scenario clearly outlines its main advantage, primary trade-off, potential risks, and any data gaps.
  • Grounded in real-world constraints. The tool never recommends crops you lack the machinery or irrigation to grow, and it keeps projected income above your set threshold. It also avoids pushing unprofitable cover crops.

For Soil and Water

  • Focus on long-term fertility. Track how many days a field stays bare alongside changes in soil carbon, nitrogen, and erosion—looking beyond just this year's profit.
  • Monthly water planning. View projected moisture deficits and irrigation requirements broken down month by month.

Accessibility

  • Zero barriers to entry. No sign-ups, installations, or special hardware needed. It runs for free right in your browser on a phone or laptop.
  • Built for every user. Available in Ukrainian and English, featuring "Simple" and "Advanced" modes as well as "Field" and "Garden" settings—making it equally useful for commercial agronomists and home gardeners.
  • Instant reporting. Generate and download a ready-to-use PDF report directly from your browser.

Transparency and Trust

  • Every number is traceable. Each metric displays its exact scientific source (such as FAO-56, IPCC, or Panagos). Team assumptions are clearly marked and can be customized to fit your reality.
  • Honest about limitations. The platform openly states what it does not model, including crop diseases, pests, and mineral fertilizers.

What is the intended impact of our project?

AGROZONE aims to help farmers choose crop rotations that hold up in hotter, drier and less predictable seasons, before they commit seed, water and money. It shows how each option performs in a typical and in a bad year, field by field. This should help farmers cut climate-related losses, use water more wisely and keep soil covered and fertile. In the long run, we want NASA Earth observations to become a normal part of everyday farm decisions, from large farms to small household plots.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did we use to develop our project?

We built AGROZONE in Python: a FastAPI back end (with Pydantic and Uvicorn) and a NumPy/SciPy simulation engine. The web interface uses plain HTML, CSS and JavaScript, with Leaflet for the map, Chart.js for charts and pdfmake for in-browser PDF reports. Data comes from the NASA POWER daily API and NASA ORNL DAAC (MODIS NDVI/EVI), plus ISRIC SoilGrids for soil properties and the Copernicus DEM via Open-Meteo for slope. We use pytest for automated tests and Playwright with Chromium for interface checks. We built a Docker image of the application and deployed it to Google Cloud Run on Google Cloud Platform (GCP), making AGROZONE accessible online through a web browser. No special hardware was needed: we developed on ordinary laptops. AI assistants helped draft parts of the code and documentation, and we as the team reviewed and tested everything we produced.

How is our project creative?

AGROZONE treats a crop rotation as a multi-year bet. It replays each option through 42 years of real NASA weather, simulating the soil-water balance and crop stress day by day, and then tests it again under a hotter, drier climate. Instead of abstract weight sliders, the farmer picks a business goal and sets hard limits, such as "income no lower than today". The tool suggests cover crops only where the farmer allows them, because few farmers will plant a crop that doesn't pay. Every result shows what you gain and what you give up with the source of each number. The same tool works for a large farm in hectares and for a household garden in ares, so NASA data reaches people who would never open a climate dataset.

What factors did our team consider?

Farm economics: income, costs and prices; cover crops are optional because they rarely pay.
Real constraints: available machinery, irrigation (rainfed, limited quota or full), tillage, mulch and manure.
Agronomy: crop-family return intervals (disease risk), sowing windows, frost and heat thresholds, legume nitrogen fixation.
Climate risk: typical and bad years, a stress test for hotter and drier conditions, and 42-year trends in heat and water deficit.
Soil health: soil-carbon change, erosion, nitrogen balance and days of bare soil.
Water: moisture deficit and irrigation demand by month.
Data quality: coarse grids (NASA POWER at about 50 km, SoilGrids at 250 m), labelled fallbacks when a source is unavailable, and offline caching.
Scientific honesty: each value is labelled as literature, derived or team assumption, and what the model leaves out is stated (pests, diseases, mineral fertiliser).
Different users: large farms in hectares and household gardens in ares, Simple and Advanced modes, Ukrainian and English.
Accessibility: works in an ordinary browser on a phone or laptop, with no sign-up and no special hardware.
Privacy: no accounts and no database; the PDF report is built in the browser.
Explainability: plain-language reasons, trade-offs, data gaps and risks for every option.
dataRefs: NASA POWER (Prediction Of Worldwide Energy Resources): daily weather data since 1981 (T2M, T2M_MAX, T2M_MIN, PRECTOTCORR, ALLSKY_SFC_SW_DWN, RH2M, WS2M)
SRTMGL1 v003 (NASA SRTM 1-arc-second Global, 30 m): elevation and slope of the field
SMAP L4 Global 3-hourly 9 km Surface and Root Zone Soil Moisture (SPL4SMGP): root zone moisture
MODIS/Terra Vegetation Indices 16-Day L3 Global 250 m (MOD13Q1 v061): NDVI/EVI
NASA ORNL DAAC MODIS/VIIRS Land Product Subsets (TESViS REST API) (MODIS)
projectRefs: FAO-56, Allen et al. 1998, Crop evapotranspiration
FAO-66, Steduto et al. 2012, Crop yield response to water
FAO-33, Doorenbos & Kassam 1979, Yield response to water
Mohler & Johnson 2009, Crop Rotation on Organic Farms
Copernicus DEM GLO-90 via the Open-Meteo Elevation API (alternative method if you don't have an Earthdata login)
